INTERVIEW: Carol Scott’s unseen photos capture a golden era of Bay Area music

INTERVIEW: Carol Scott’s unseen photos capture a golden era of Bay Area music

  • Features
  • Highlights
  • Interview
July 27, 2026
byKiren Kaur
1
Mick Jagger performs with the Rolling Stones at Oakland Coliseum in Oakland on July 26, 1978. This photo is displayed in the permanent collection of the National Portrait Gallery in London. Photo: Carol Scott.

Carol Scott, 78, spends her days alongside her daughter, going through archives of photos from 40 years ago. Some of them she’s not seen before and others she’s now looking at with a new lens.

Photographic& Digital Arts

Discover more
photographs
Concert
Concerts & Music Festivals

The photos, taken between 1977 and 1985, include candid snaps and intimate peaks into the souls of Jerry Garcia, Etta James and Rod Stewart, Bonnie Raitt, Prince, Frank Zappa, John Lee Hooker, Ray Charles… the list goes on.

The past few years for Scott have sparked a newfound excitement for her  photography, as many are seeing her photos for the first time. As she digs up more, she uncovers new stories of artists who’ve left their mark in the Bay Area.

Inspired by her great-grandfather, a painter and photographer himself, the London-born Scott was driven by her fondness of American blues and rock and roll to pursue photography.

“I felt him egging me on, encouraging me,” Scott said over a recent call from her home in Oakland. “I thought it might be a way to earn a living to support myself.”

Discover more
Online Image Galleries
Music & Audio
Rock Music

Scott bought a one-way ticket to New York in 1970 before hitchhiking west. She ended up in Berkeley because she’d met a musician from the Bay Area while traveling in Morocco two years prior. He’d said she could stay with him. She spend her first three years traveling the  U.S., also living briefly in Montana and Tennessee.

TouristDestinations

Scott bought a 35 mm Nikkormat camera and learned to develop film. After having her daughter, Cameron Scott, the two returned to Berkeley in 1975 to start fresh. There, Scott met Richard Blair, a photographer who mentored her. With his help, she turned her daughter’s closet into a darkroom and enrolled in Oakland’s Laney College to “study properly.”

Her regular haunt was the Keystone in Berkeley. She’d buy a cheap ticket to the small club and work as close as possible to the stage, sometimes using her camera to help stand her ground against others who tried to push her out of the way. Eventually she met the right people, working backstage and meeting the performers, sometimes taking an intimate portrait.

“The more I did, the more I wanted to do it,” said Scott, her waitressed to make ends meet. “This is the  music I’ve grown up loving and now these people are right on my doorstep.”

Along the way, she formed friendships with the likes of John Lee Hooker and Muddy Waters, Van Morrison and Frank Zappa — with whom she’d stay up all night listening to old soul records. She also built up on-stage photo portfolios of several artists like Jerry Garcia and Maria Muldaur, a 1960s and 1970s Greenwich Village, New York folk music icon, who’s best known for 1973 hit “Midnight at the Oasis.” Muldaur moved to Marin in the late ’70s and often performed with the Jerry Garcia band.

“When I saw the photos, I was completely blown away!” Muldaur said in an email, noting that she only recently became familiar with Scott’s work — just like everyone else. “[They are] among the most wonderful photos ever taken of me. Her photos manage to capture artists in action, in a very natural and organic way that completely conveys the very spirit of the music being made in the moment. I’ve been blessed to be photographed by some of the best photographers in the business over the years, but these photos Carol took of me are among my very favorite. I’m glad to see her fine work is finally being recognized!”

Where some might see a groupie, Scott said the artists she photographed saw her as an artist and entrepreneur, showing her respect.

At many venues, like Oakland Coliseum and the Cow Palace, Scott wasn’t a credentialed photographer — but she got her shots anyway by sneaking her camera and gear in deliberate ways, including hiding her long telephoto lens down the back of a leotard.

Scott’s current photography collection is on display for the first time in the East Bay at Oakland’s Rockridge Cafe, highlighting iconic artists of rock,  blues, country, punk and jazz. The walls of the cafe are adorned with her photos of Prince, Ray Charles, Willie Nelson and other American icons through Aug. 5.

Photographic& Digital Arts

But Scott’s most famous  photo is on permanent display at the National Portrait Gallery in London: A snap of Mick Jagger with his guitar peeking through over his hip like a Tommy gun, at Oakland Coliseum. She took the photo at a surprise Rolling Stones show on July 26, 1978, on Jagger’s 35th birthday.

Again, she was just a fan in the crowd, and likened the experience to “going to battle” because of her height disadvantage.

“Everyone seemed so much taller than myself,” Scott said. “I thought I was going to have to give up, and then a man next to me just suddenly lifted me up on his shoulders without saying anything. I just took pictures.”

Magazine

In 1980, Scott went to London with her portfolio and met with Colin Ford, the curator of the National Portrait Gallery. Ford purchased one of her Jagger prints, telling her that it “’was the most romantic picture'” of the rocker he’d ever seen.

At first, the image went on display without attribution. Even Scott forgot it was there. It wasn’t until someone who visited the museum and recognized her work did she get proper credit.

Despite her prolific work, the Rockridge show as just Scott’s third ever. In 2024 and 2025, some of her photos were shown alongside the art of Jerry Garcia at Sausalito Center for the Arts (SCA), something she saw as “a big honor.”

Photographic& Digital Arts

SCA Executive Director Shiva Pakdel said the photos have been a hit with visitors each time.

“Carol’s  photography is really amazing because for years she’s taken these photographs and she hadn’t shown them anywhere,” Pakdel said. “They lived on film and in her camera. … She has a big following here now. There’s a whole bunch of people that show up over and over again and they look for her images. … Her photography is very unique.”

For 40 years, Scott’s negatives and slides sat in that same closet. She didn’t know what to do with them.

“It was only two or three years ago [that] Cameron said ‘Look, we’ve really got to do something about your pictures,’” Scott said. “I didn’t know where to start. [Photography is] all digital nowadays.”

With her daughter’s help, Scott began parsing  through the negatives and slides. She credits her daughter for pushing her to do it and share the photos with others.

Photographic& Digital Arts

“She’s helped bring them out to the world,” she said.

Scott doesn’t  photograph concerts anymore. At 45, she started facing vision problems, which forced her to wear glasses. Being used to balancing the camera against her forehead, this posed an obstacle. Then digital cameras came along, and Scott said she “wasn’t interested in getting into learning how to use a digital camera.” She became a paralegal, working in Oakland and San Francisco.

She wants people to remember that she captured a significant time in Bay Area history on cellulose acetate. She said she hoped people remember those artists and those concerts as fondly as she does. She also hopes her snaps inspire others to pursue their artistic interests, leaning on their mentors along the way.

“It was incredible that the camera could capture a moment and be preserved forever in a photograph,” Scott said. “I’ve captured something from the past. It hasn’t gone away. You can look at the picture today, and you could feel very alive as at the time it was taken.”

More of Scott’s work are available to view at Sausalito Center for the Arts, while a handful of her photos of Jerry Garcia and the Grateful Dead are on exhibition at Equator Coffees in Sausalito through Aug. 15.
